introduction: On this Sunday, the Letter to the Hebrews defines faith as the assurance of things hoped for, and recalls Abraham, who set out not knowing where he was going. In the Gospel, Jesus tells his little flock not to be afraid, for the Father is pleased to give them the Kingdom; he urges us to be ready, like servants waiting for their master's return. Let us live by faith and keep our lamps burning.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Father is pleased to give us the Kingdom. Let us bring him our prayers with faith.
intentions: For the Church, the little flock of Christ: that she may not be afraid but trust in the Father's care. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who hold responsibility in the Church and in society: that they may be faithful and wise stewards. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who set out into the unknown, migrants and those starting a new life: that they may go forward with faith. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are afraid of the future: that they may find peace in God's promises. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that our treasure may be in heaven, and our hearts with it. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Faithful God, you call us to be ready for the coming of your Son. Keep our lamps burning, strengthen our faith, and bring us to the city you have prepared for us. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Where your treasure is
reflection.body:
The Letter to the Hebrews gives a famous definition: "faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen." Then it gives an example. Abraham, called by God, "went out, not knowing where he went." He lived in tents as a stranger, "looking for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God." Abraham and Sarah "all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar." Faith means trusting God's promises even before we see them fulfilled.

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks tenderly to his disciples: "Don't be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom." Because the Kingdom is a gift, they can be generous: "Sell what you have and give gifts to the needy." And he gives a principle that applies to every life: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Then Jesus calls us to be ready. "Let your waist be dressed and your lamps burning." He tells of servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding. And he adds a surprising detail: when the master finds them watching, "he will dress himself, make them recline, and will come and serve them." The Lord we wait for comes to serve us.

Peter asks whether this is for everyone. Jesus speaks of a faithful steward, who cares for others while the master is away. Responsibility comes with gifts: "To whomever much is given, of him will much be required."

This week, ask yourself where your treasure is: what do you spend your time, money and thoughts on? Make one choice to store up treasure in heaven: give something to someone in need. And keep your lamp burning through daily prayer.
